content: Hexosaminidase A, also referred to as HEXA, is an enzyme in humans encoded by the HEXA gene, which is located on chromosome 15. This enzyme, in conjunction with the GM2 activator protein, facilitates the breakdown of GM2 gangliosides and other molecules containing terminal N-acetylhexosamines. Hexosaminidase A is a heterodimer composed of two subunits: an alpha subunit (encoded by the HEXA gene) and a beta subunit (encoded by the HEXB gene). Mutations in the HEXB gene, which encodes the beta subunit, are commonly associated with Sandhoff disease. Conversely, mutations in the HEXA gene, which encodes the alpha subunit, impair the hydrolysis of GM2 gangliosides, leading to Tay–Sachs disease. The alpha and beta subunits of hexosaminidase A both have the ability to cleave GalNAc residues. However, only the alpha subunit can hydrolyze GM2 gangliosides. This specificity is due to the presence of a critical residue, Arg-424, in the alpha subunit, which is essential for binding the N-acetylneuraminic acid residue of GM2 gangliosides. Additionally, the alpha subunit contains a unique loop structure formed by the amino acids Gly-280, Ser-281, Glu-282, and Pro-283. This loop is absent in the beta subunit but is crucial for the binding of the GM2 activator protein (GM2AP) to the alpha subunit. Together, Arg-424 and the loop structure enable the alpha subunit to hydrolyze GM2 gangliosides into GM3 gangliosides by removing the N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) residue. Numerous mutations can lead to hexosaminidase A deficiency, including gene deletions, nonsense mutations, and missense mutations. Tay–Sachs disease occurs when hexosaminidase A loses its functional capacity. Individuals with Tay–Sachs disease are unable to remove the GalNAc residue from GM2 gangliosides, resulting in the accumulation of GM2 gangliosides in the brain at levels 100 to 1,000 times higher than normal. Over 100 different mutations have been identified in infantile cases of Tay–Sachs disease alone. The most common mutation, found in over 80% of Tay–Sachs patients, involves a four-base pair insertion (TATC) in exon 11 of the HEXA gene. This insertion introduces an early stop codon, leading to hexosaminidase A deficiency. Children with Tay–Sachs disease typically die between the ages of two and six due to complications such as aspiration and pneumonia. The disease causes cerebral degeneration, blindness, flaccid extremities, and seizures. Currently, there is no cure for Tay–Sachs disease. The HEXA gene encodes the lysosomal enzyme beta-hexosaminidase, which, in combination with the GM2 activator protein, is responsible for breaking down GM2 gangliosides within lysosomes. Defects in the HEXA gene prevent this degradation, leading to the accumulation of toxic substances in brain and spinal cord cells. This fatal genetic disorder is known as Tay–Sachs disease. Because the HEXA gene defect primarily affects neural cells, patients with this mutation experience rapid deterioration of motor and mental functions, typically resulting in death around the age of three or four. A knockout mouse model, in which the HEXA gene is inactivated or damaged, has been used to study the effects of HEXA deficiency. These mice exhibit many of the same symptoms as human Tay–Sachs patients, with one notable difference: the distribution of GM2 ganglioside accumulation in the brain differs between the mice and human patients. This model has facilitated research into potential gene therapies for HEXA defects. In one study, researchers successfully restored beta-hexosaminidase levels and eliminated toxic cellular buildup in mice by using a non-replicating herpes simplex virus vector to deliver the missing gene.
